claims.text: Unmodified CoCrFeNi exhibits deteriorating tribological performance over the stated temperature range.
A PVD-deposited coating can be functionally graded from an upper MoS2-rich layer to an underlying Cr2O3-rich layer.
The MoS2-rich surface provides easy shear at room temperature.
Easy shear in layered MoS2 reduces low-temperature friction.
At elevated temperatures, an underlying Cr2O3 phase emerges or becomes tribologically dominant.
The high-temperature Cr2O3 phase forms a stable, self-healing lubricious film.
A Cr2O3-based film resists wear because it is robust and thermally stable.
The MoS2 layer transitions into a Cr2O3-based film as temperature increases.
Depth-dependent adaptation of the graded coating accommodates changes in operating conditions.
The graded coating will maintain low friction on CoCrFeNi from 25 °C to 800 °C.
The coated CoCrFeNi will have lower coefficients of friction than uncoated CoCrFeNi across the entire 25–800 °C range.
The coated CoCrFeNi will have improved wear resistance relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi across the entire 25–800 °C range.
The coating will remain intact and operative under the prescribed variations in load and environment.
Uncoated CoCrFeNi shows increased friction and accelerated wear, especially at higher temperatures.
The coating will be effective in oxidizing environments from 25 °C to 800 °C under moderate-to-high engineered loads.

contradictions.description: The coating is initially described as containing distinct MoS2-rich and Cr2O3-rich depth regions, but other fields describe a MoS2-to-Cr2O3 transition. These are different mechanisms—exposure or dominance of a pre-existing Cr2O3 layer versus chemical conversion—and the hypothesis does not resolve which is proposed.
Performance is claimed under varying environmental conditions, but the stated conditions and experiment specify only an oxidizing atmosphere, so environmental variation is not actually tested.
